sentences.text: Two different costs, and only one of them is real.
Implementation: small.

The recommended version is roughly 25–35 lines across three files — a new resyncTo on FishSwimPresentation (six scalar assignments), a resetTo on FishSurfaceController that's an extraction of two lines already running in the constructor rather than new logic, and a two-line call site on the false→true edge in SchoolingFish.setVisible.
The four-line facing-only variant is smaller still and touches one file.
Low risk either way: nothing changes for a fish that stays visible, so the steady-state render path is untouched.
Runtime, the resync itself: negligible.

It fires once per invisible→visible transition per fish, not per frame, and the expensive part — setInitialSegments rebuilding the drag chain — costs about what one frame of that fish's normal spine solve costs.
So each appearance pays roughly one extra frame of its own work, once.
Even with a few dozen transitions per second across 300 fish, that's noise.
Runtime, the margin bump: this is the part that actually costs anything.
Raising viewportCulling.marginUnits from 1 to ~4 widens the band of fish that get a full-rate render every frame.

The cost scales with the added band area around the viewport, not with the margin directly — so it's a percentage of your current visible-fish count, and it's paid every frame forever, unlike the resync.
Whether that's 5% or 25% more rendered fish depends on your viewport dimensions in world units, which I'd want measured rather than guessed.
There are 2 different costs: code-wise, and performance-wise.
Code-wise, it's small.
The recommended version is roughly 25-35 lines across three files.
Performance-wise, the margin bump is the one worth looking at.
Raising viewportCulling.marginUnits from 1 to ~4 increases the number of fish that are rendered at full rate every frame.
The exact amount depends on the banded area around your viewport in world units.
I would measure this rather than guess.
Meanwhile, the resync itself is negligible.
It fires once per invisible -> visible transition per fish.
Even with a few dozen transitions per second across 300 fish, that's noise.
Three sessile organisms for Remora's rock and sediment: a bed of cylindrical seagrass blades, a crumpled translucent sheet alga, and a planar netted gorgonian.
Each is drawn in profile in its own attachment frame, root floating just above the frame edge, with no substrate — placement in the game supplies the rock.
All three sample one shared slow current and differ only in stiffness and lag: the thin blades answer first, the broad sheet lags, and the calcified fan barely moves.
Use the sliders to find a default for the entity definition; the very faint shape behind each specimen is its rest pose.
